Reaction kinetics and mass transfer synergistically enhanced the electrochemical oxidation performance of porous SiC/Ta/BDD electrodes in a flow-through reactor
Aberrant one-carbon metabolism and ancestral genetics underlie edematous severe acute malnutrition
articles.abstract: Abstract Edematous severe childhood malnutrition is distinct from the non-edematous form of malnutrition and remains a major cause of under-five mortality. Its etiology remains unclear, although aberrant one-carbon metabolism has emerged as a potential contributor. Here, we assess genetic variants at loci known to influence one-carbon metabolism, and determine their association with edematous malnutrition in Jamaica and Malawi. Six loci show evidence of association, including four related to homocysteine and folate metabolism - AHCYL1 , PRICKLE2 , GABBR2 , and PLD2 , with SNPs at the latter three also having direct effects on homocysteine-related metabolites in Mendelian Randomization. Collectively, one-carbon metabolism-related variants were significantly associated with edematous malnutrition (z = 3.2), with population differences linked to a shared East African genetic ancestry and distinct signatures of selection. These findings strengthen evidence implicating aberrant one-carbon metabolism in edematous malnutrition and highlight the utility of cell-free DNA, intra-continental admixture, and population genetics for mapping disease risk.

articles.title: Electronic tuning of dynamic imine bonds enables programmable pore gating in metal–organic frameworks
Elevated prenatal IL-6 levels disrupt early patterns of hippocampal electrical activity and chloride homeostasis by targeting GABAergic signaling at perinatal stage
articles.abstract: Abstract Early patterns of neuronal electrical activity are fundamental for driving critical developmental processes, including neuronal maturation and synapse formation. While genetic programs are key in orchestrating these events, the influence of environmental stressors remains poorly defined. Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy induces a systemic cytokine surge that can profoundly impact fetal brain development, increasing the risk of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we show that maternal elevation of interleukin-6 (IL-6) – a key cytokine upregulated during MIA – perturbs early hippocampal electrical activity in male offspring during the first postnatal week, a critical window for circuit formation. By triggering a STAT3-dependent modulation of early GABAergic synaptic transmission, IL-6 disrupts chloride homeostasis, causing a premature shift in the developmental GABA polarity switch. Our findings reveal a direct link between maternal immune signaling and early GABA-driven network maturation, providing insights into how inflammatory events during pregnancy may predispose male offspring to neurodevelopmental disorders.

articles.title: Tissue composition shapes differential skeletal integration strategies during axolotl limb regeneration
articles.abstract: Abstract Limb regeneration requires rebuilding the missing structures and integrating them with stump tissues. Osteoclast-mediated tissue resorption is essential for skeletal integration during regeneration. However, it is unknown if skeletal tissue composition impacts its resorption and, if so, how it is regulated. Here, we show that osteoclast-mediated skeletal resorption is activated in amputations damaging the diaphysis, but not the epiphysis, of skeletal elements. We found that amputations in the calcified diaphysis trigger the sustained expression of RANKL and the chemokine Loc483 , and that the latter is sufficient to induce osteoclast presence in non-resorbing amputations. Finally, our data suggests that the transcriptomic profile of the apical epithelial cap is impacted by the tissues injured by the amputation. Overall, our work reveals that tissue composition at the amputation plane shapes adaptations of the regenerative program, which ultimately contribute to the near-seamless tissue integration of the regenerating axolotl limb regardless of the amputation position.

articles.title:
Trimester-Specific
Associations of Prenatal Heat Exposure
with Neonatal Amino Acid and Acylcarnitine Profiles
articles.abstract: Abstract It remains unclear whether prenatal heat exposure is associated with newborn metabolic profiles. Therefore, based on 4714 mother–infant pairs in Shanghai, we aimed to investigate the trimester-specific associations of prenatal heat exposure with neonatal amino acid (AA) and acylcarnitine (AC) profiles. Heat exposure was defined using the 90th percentile of trimester-specific temperature distributions from the ERA5-Land data set. For AAs, glutamate showed consistently positive associations across three trimesters, whereas phenylalanine, tyrosine, leucine, arginine, and citrulline showed consistently negative associations; other AAs exhibited trimester-specific patterns. For ACs, C2, C4, and C16 showed consistently negative associations, while a chain-length-dependent pattern was observed: short-chain ACs were predominantly negatively associated, whereas most medium- and long-chain ACs reversed to positive associations in the second and third trimesters. Network topology analysis revealed stronger metabolite correlation structures in the heat-exposed group across all trimesters, with AA-AC pairs accounting for the largest proportion of differential correlations. Distributed lag nonlinear models suggested susceptible windows at gestational weeks 10–17 and 25–27 for AAs, and weeks 8–14 and 26–34 for ACs. Overall, prenatal heat exposure was significantly associated with multiple neonatal AAs and ACs, with distinct trimester-specific patterns and a denser intermetabolite correlation network in the heat-exposed group.

articles.title:
Beyond Equilibrium:
Tracing Redox-Driven Pathways
That Shape Aqueous and Mineral Chemistry
articles.abstract: Abstract Numerous aqueous and geochemical systems host elements in multiple redox states, with wide ranging implications such as their influence on the formation/dissolution of minerals, water toxicity, and nutrient cycling. To uncover governing mechanisms and complex chemical interactions in geochemical systems, reactive-transport models have increasingly gained importance. However, their predictive capabilities remain limited because existing approaches struggle to accurately account for the full complexities of redox reactions. Here, we develop a reactive-transport framework that leverages recent advances in thermodynamic modeling, speciation chemistry, and redox kinetics. Distinct from traditional models, we uniquely treat redox kinetics along with transport as transient phenomena, decoupled from Gibbs free energy minimization. By ensuring ionic concentrations are governed by nonequilibrium rate laws, this approach allows predicting the tempo-spatial distribution of speciation and precipitation of species across oxidation states. We illustrate the versatility of our framework through two case studies: manganese speciation in natural waters and the fate of dissolved iron in aqueous/porous media. Our framework significantly enhances the modeling of a diverse range of redox-sensitive environments.

articles.title:
Receptor Binding
Drives Toxicokinetic Processes: Insights
from Two Amphipod Species Exposed to Insecticides Targeting the Nicotinic
Acetylcholine Receptor
articles.abstract: Abstract Insecticides targeting nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are used because of their high neuroactive efficacy. However, they can also exert substantial toxic pressure on nontarget aquatic invertebrates. A previous study suggested that irreversible receptor binding is the main driver of thiacloprid bioaccumulation. To determine whether the observed elimination resistance applies to other nAChR-binding insecticides and species, this study investigates five compounds from different substance classes that target nAChRs. Using the two amphipod species, Hyalella azteca and Gammarus pulex, toxicokinetic experiments were combined with assessing receptor binding in vivo and in vitro. The three N-cyanoamidines and N-nitroguanidine neonicotinoids (thiacloprid, acetamiprid, and imidacloprid) and the metabolite imidacloprid-olefin showed resistance toward elimination (i.e., over 15 days of depuration in both amphipod species). This observation could be well described by a two-compartment toxicokinetic (TK)-receptor model (>0.89 R2) with integrated irreversible binding. In contrast, the butenolide flupyradifurone was fully eliminated, and the organic biocide spinosad was eliminated significantly but slowly, both fitted well with a one-compartment TK model (>0.71 R2). These findings demonstrate that receptor-binding specificity and affinity are highly compound class dependent. Although no direct link between receptor binding and acute toxicity could be established, elimination resistance indicates a risk for delayed, sublethal effects that should be critically considered in regulatory risk assessment.

articles.title:
Condensation Sink
Efficiency of Atmospheric Particles
Regulated by Their Chemical Compositions and Hygroscopicity
articles.abstract: Abstract Condensation sink (CS) from atmospheric pre-existing particles is a crucial limiting factor for the occurrence of new particle formation (NPF). However, intense NPF events occur frequently in polluted urban areas despite high CS levels. Here, to address this discrepancy, we introduce an efficiency coefficient ε (ε = CSeff/CScal) to quantify the CS efficiency of pre-existing particles toward gaseous H2SO4, where CScal was calculated under the assumption of irreversible uptake. Results demonstrate that ε strongly depends on hygroscopicity and chemical compositions of particles. Under dry conditions, the ε of pure organic particles was less than that of pure inorganic particles, but high humidity increased ε for both. For mixed organic-inorganic particles, the ε was adjusted together by particle chemical compositions and humidity. Exploratory measurements further revealed a decline in CS efficiency for gaseous HIO3. Incorporating ε into field data and models improves cluster survival predictions and sub-3-nm particle formation simulations, potentially explaining the NPF mystery in megacities under high CS and leading to more accurate modeling of NPF impacts.

articles.title:
Designing SynComs
for Resilience beyond Efficiency
Spontaneous ferromagnetic Fe–La geminal atoms with spin and coordination modulation for acidic oxygen reduction
A nanosystem manipulates angiocrine signaling for cardioprotection in male mice by relocalizing endothelial exosomes
Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
articles.abstract: Abstract Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8–41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0–62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

articles.title: Author Correction: Versatile molecular tools enabling customizable DNA methylation editing in Arabidopsis
Mapping cell-type-specific spatial gene programs uncovers tissue architecture and microenvironment organization
Genome-reduced Aridivitia evolved predation to thrive in Earth’s oligotrophic depths
articles.abstract: Abstract Deep soils represent one of Earth’s largest yet most enigmatic microbial habitats, where survival strategies under extreme oligotrophy remain poorly understood. Here, we report the Aridivitia group, a globally distributed bacterial lineage enriched in oligotrophic soils and thriving down to 22 m depth across sites in the United States and China. Despite its genome reduction (average size ~2.9 Mb), Aridivitia exhibits high metabolic flexibility in utilizing diverse carbon and energy sources. Cellular, genomic, and metatranscriptomic evidence, including small cell and genome sizes, host-associated metabolism, and the active expression of attachment- and attack-associated surface structures such as Tad pili and pore-forming toxins, indicate a predatory lifestyle in Aridivitia. Ancestral genome reconstruction reveals that Aridivitia originated as free-living mixotrophs, but subsequently lost the ability to fix carbon as they evolved a predatory lifestyle. Collectively, Aridivitia exemplifies a unique evolutionary strategy that reconciles genome reduction with functional versatility, expanding our understanding of microbial adaptation and evolution at the energetic limits of life.

articles.title: Spectral sensing at a glance
Shifting balance between habitat and climate in boreal biodiversity patterns across space, time and taxa
Luminal geometry and coiled coil length determine submembrane localization of type II transmembrane Golgi proteins
Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
articles.abstract: Abstract Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

articles.title: EphrinA4/EphA4 controls blood pressure via arterial sympathetic innervation in male mice
Integrated multi-omics identifies distinct immune signatures with diagnostic and therapeutic implications in immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis
articles.abstract: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-myocarditis) is a rare but frequently fatal immune-related adverse event. A comprehensive understanding of the cellular and molecular determinants driving ICI-myocarditis is essential for improving diagnostic precision and developing targeted interventions. We delineate the immune landscape of ICI-myocarditis via scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, Olink proteomics, and multiplex cytokine profiling. We demonstrate that high levels of baseline ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells are linked to the proinflammatory features of monocytes and in vitro experiments confirm the existence of circulating ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells with a high potential to induce cardiomyocyte apoptosis, supporting their pathogenic potential for cardiomyocyte cytotoxicity. Notably, intercellular crosstalk between these subsets is possibly mediated via the CCL2-CCR2 axis, and its blockade attenuated ICI-induced cardiac injury in vivo. Based on the inflammatory signature in ICI-myocarditis, we develop an 8-protein custom panel with promising performance in distinguishing ICI-myocarditis from other ICIs-treated controls. JAK-STAT pathway activation promotes inflammatory programs in both ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells and monocytes. Furthermore, JAK-STAT inhibition ameliorates cardiac dysfunction and inflammatory infiltration while enhancing the response to anti-PD-1 therapy in mouse models. In summary, this study implicates immune-pathogenic features of ICI-myocarditis and provides a possible basis for future therapies.

articles.title: Fever enhances host bacterial defence while limiting mitochondrial damage
articles.abstract: Abstract Infection triggers the fever response, but the response’s effect on antimicrobial peptide (AMP) function remains unknown. We discovered that human AMP LL-37 antibacterial activity is temperature-dependent and were curious as to why. Its temperature dependence is not an accident, as AMPs from other animals with different body temperatures have distinct temperature sensitivities. We find that AMP temperature sensitivities are tuned to animals’ body temperatures, and that for animals able to raise their body temperature, this is used to increase the AMP’s antibacterial efficacy. This effect reflects a balance between optimizing antibacterial killing while minimizing mitochondrial damage. In contrast, cold-blooded animals that are unable to raise their body temperature use a different strategy to avoid mitochondrial damage. Together, this study suggests that fever is beneficial for antimicrobial defense by raising AMP activity towards bacteria while reducing mitochondrial damage when pathogens are absent.

articles.title: Signatures of bi-altermagnetism revealed by sublattice-specific circular dichroism in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
Orientation tomography of lanthanide-doped nanoprobes by polarization-resolved micro-spectroscopy
articles.abstract: Abstract Quantifying three-dimensional (3D) orientation is critical for understanding self-assembly and collective behavior in soft matter and biological systems. Moreover, orientational analysis of anisotropic particles can characterize locally applied forces in fluids. We present a methodology for 3D orientation tomography based on polarization-resolved spectroscopy of lanthanide-doped nanorods exhibiting multiple emission dipoles, enabling 3D orientation measurements from a single viewing angle. We develop a confocal imaging setup optimized for lanthanide luminescence and a theoretical framework to extract both the local director and order parameter in nanorod assemblies. The technique achieves 0.5 μm lateral and 1 μm axial spatial resolution and is demonstrated in dense nematic liquid-crystal assemblies, resolving complex 3D topological structures, and in microfluidic flows, mapping alignment under hydrodynamic shear. This approach provides a versatile platform for quantitative studies of collective orientation, self-assembly mechanics, and alignment induced by external forces, and can be extended to other lanthanide-labeled particles and molecular probes.

articles.title: On predictability of slip, rupture geometry, and speed of the 2025 M7.8 Mandalay, Myanmar, earthquake
articles.abstract: Abstract The 2025 M 7.8 Mandalay earthquake ruptured ~480 km of the Sagaing Fault, producing one of the longest strike-slip events documented and impacting a vulnerable region. Here we combine remote sensing observations and numerical modeling to show that the subsurface fault geometry and slip distribution could be anticipated from pre-event observations. Along-strike variations in coseismic and interseismic deformation reveal a helix-shaped fault geometry. The average coseismic slip equals or exceeds the interseismic slip deficit, consistent with a minimally slip-predictable model. We generate an ensemble of 3D dynamic rupture models, constrained by the best-fit static slip model, then discriminate among them using independent space-geodetic, seismic, and near-field video observations. The preferred scenario begins bilaterally, then transitions to unilateral southward supershear propagation at depth, while shallow rupture remains subshear. These dynamics are shaped by localized stress heterogeneity and low fracture energy, characteristic of a structurally mature fault zone. Our approach can inform rupture scenarios in understudied regions.

articles.title:
Novel
Insight into Organoarsenic Degradation and Inorganic
Arsenic Sequestration in Ferrate Treatment: Unraveling the Role of
Active Fe–As Complexes at the Molecular Level
articles.abstract: Abstract Efficiently removing organoarsenic contaminants like p-Aminophenylarsonic acid (pASA) with their toxic inorganic byproducts remains a major challenge. Ferrate [Fe(VI)] can oxidize organoarsenic and immobilize inorganic arsenic, but the molecular mechanisms linking these functions are unclear. Here, using theoretical computational spectroscopy and stopped-flow analysis, we identified a critical pathway mediated by Fe(V/IV)–O-As(III) intermediates (INTs) that bridges oxidative degradation and heterogeneous sequestration. X-band EPR further confirmed the INTs (g-factors = 2.006, 1.928, 1.712), with rhombic peaks and quadruple hyperfine splitting. These INTs form barrierlessly between Fe(VI/V) and ·As(III)O(OH)2 released upon C–As bond cleavage in pASA. The thus-formed INTs exhibit superior reactivity to Fe(VI/V/IV), enabling more effective organoarsenic degradation and As(III) oxidation via outer-sphere electron transfer. Additionally, these INTs facilitate highly efficient inner-sphere electron transfer, forming Fe(III/II)–O-As(V) complexes that directly evolve into As-bearing Fe nanoparticles via Fe–O–As bond formation, a process with a lower energy barrier. The abundance of INTs during pASA degradation can be regulated by modulating Fe(VI) decomposition kinetics using common reagents: H2O2 accelerates and NaClO delays Fe(VI) decomposition. The Fe(VI)/NaClO system achieved 88% total As removal, higher than the 72% for Fe(VI)/H2O2 and 78% for Fe(VI) alone, and exhibited enhanced As–Fe coordination, indicating improved sequestration. Overall, this work reveals a pivotal mechanistic bridge in metalloid contaminant removal, offering new insights for designing oxidation-sequestration synergy in environmental remediation.

articles.title:
Fluoropolymers across
Their Life Cycle: Why “Emissions
Reduction” Is Not “Safe”

Ice
Converts Phenols
into Persistent Mineral-Bound
Polymers
articles.abstract: Abstract Freezing fundamentally alters how minerals transform dissolved phenols in cold environments. As water freezes, solutes are excluded from the crystal lattice and concentrated into microscopic pockets of unfrozen liquid, creating reaction conditions far more extreme than those of bulk solution. Here, we compare catechol oxidation on a key soil manganese oxide under freeze–thaw versus room-temperature conditions. Freezing redirects products from soluble humic-like substances to thermally stable, mineral-bound polymers. Freeze–thaw conditions removed over 50% of dissolved organic carbon within 24 h compared to less than 10% at room temperature, with solid-phase carbon increasing over 50-fold. The attenuation of the effect with increasing salinity is consistent with freeze-concentration as a key driver and indicates that the pathway should be strongest in freshwater and low-salinity frozen environments. Freeze–thaw conditions also converted preformed soluble products into mineral-bound forms, demonstrating that the process operates on a range of substrates. These findings reveal an unrecognized abiotic carbon stabilization pathway that could operate when microbial decomposition is suppressed by freezing with direct implications for carbon dynamics in permafrost and seasonally frozen environments.

articles.title: Establishment of a Novel Alternative Method Using the Gobiocypris rarus AhR for Toxicity Testing of the Dioxin-like Potency of Halogenated Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons
articles.abstract: Abstract Halogenated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (HPAHs) often exhibit distinct toxicity and mechanisms relative to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), yet most remain unassessed, particularly for dioxin-like effects mediated by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). This study characterized three rare minnow AhRs and established an efficient AhR-activation screening assay (using graAhR2, EC50 = 2.53 nM and Z′ factor = 0.58), and evaluated 40 HPAHs/PAHs with preliminary activity screening and ecotoxicity considered. HPAHs showed a median IC50 of 1.15 × 10–4 M for cellular viability (parent PAHs: 4.29 × 10–4 M), indicating greater cellular toxicity. Nine compounds were AhR-active. Notably, halogenated fluorene and pyrene exhibited AhR activation, whereas the parent did not. 4-bromobenz[a]anthracene exhibited 2028-fold higher activation potency than the parent. Acute toxicity (cell viability IC50) and AhR activation potency (EC50) exhibited a weak correlation, R2 = 0.21 and P = 0.22 in COS-7 cells, implying little AhR contribution to acute toxicity. All HPAHs/PAHs shared a similar binding direction within the AhR. AhR-active compounds possessed greater affinity than inactive ones (P = 0.0032). For instance, in fluorene-based HPAHs, a binding pose more similar to 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) may confer stronger activation potency. The results support the need for a tiered risk evaluation of HPAHs, e.g., considering acute and long-term aspects, and integrating dioxin-like potency into relevant regulatory frameworks, e.g., the toxic equivalency factor (TEF) or similar ones.

articles.title:
Why
Can Cross-End Point Transfer Fail in Computational
Toxicology? Diagnosing Decision-Structure Incompatibility across 13
End Points under Scaffold-Held-Out Evaluation
articles.abstract: Abstract Cross-end point information sharing may improve toxicity prediction when labeled data are limited, but biologically related end points are not necessarily predictively compatible. We evaluated transfer strategies across 13 toxicity end points using scaffold-disjoint repeated cross-validation with strict leakage control. The benchmark compared data-level pooling with higher-level approaches, including stacking, multitask learning, model-agnostic meta-learning, and frozen-encoder feature augmentation (FEFA). Direct cross-prediction between different end points was generally weak, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.525 across 156 ordered end point pairs, indicating limited standalone portability of end point-specific decision rules. Global data merging reduced macro-average ROC-AUC by 0.0287 relative to end point-specific baselines, whereas several higher-level approaches produced modest gains. The strongest macro-average improvements were observed for stacking (+0.0101 ROC-AUC) and FEFA (+0.0070), although effects varied substantially among end points. Additional decision-structure and representation analyses were consistent with transfer performance being strategy- and target-dependent rather than determined by biological relatedness alone. These findings support leakage-controlled, end point-specific evaluation when using cross-end point learning for chemical toxicity assessment and caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous toxicity data.

articles.title:
Decadal Biochar
Legacy Stabilizes Paddy Soil Carbon
by Reshaping Redox-Driven Reactive Oxygen Species Dynamics
articles.abstract: Abstract Biochar (BC) displays great potential in stabilizing soil organic carbon, yet its decadal legacy for carbon preservation under redox oscillations remains unclear. The study comprehensively investigated how decadal BC (D-BC) application restrained carbon mineralization of paddy soil via reshaping reactive oxygen species (ROS) dynamics. In situ fluorescence imaging and quantification results showed that D-BC soil inhibited hydroxyl radical (•OH) generation by 22.3% than fresh BC (F-BC) input soil, but elevating hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and superoxide (O2•–) accumulation by 36.2% and 25.4% during redox oscillation, respectively. This resulted from its weakened microbial iron reduction and the lower reactivity of Fe(II), which significantly limited Fenton reactions. In contrast, a shift in the microbial community to redox-adapted taxa, lower catalase activity, and enriched dissolved inorganic carbon collectively facilitated the biogenic origin of H2O2 in D-BC soil. Scavenging and correlation analyses revealed that reduced •OH generation led to net suppression in CO2 emission from D-BC soil by >30% via upregulating the enzymatic latch, while enhanced H2O2 accumulation imposed oxidative stress on carbon-degrading microbes. Laboratory verifications confirmed the roles of surface oxidation and persistent free radical attenuation of aged BC in ROS redistribution. The failure of decadal straw (D-Straw) return to reproduce these phenomena suggested that the decadal BC legacy stemmed from a particular redox impact, rather than exogenous carbon input alone. The findings uncovered a new mechanism of BC-induced carbon stability, advancing understanding of the carbon cycle within redox-dynamic zones.

articles.title:
Identification
of
Novel PFAS Transformation Products
in AFFF-Impacted Surface and Groundwater
articles.abstract: Abstract The widespread use of Aqueous Film-Forming Foams (AFFF) has left thousands of contaminated “hotspots” across North America. In Canada, only 25 per-/polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are regulated in drinking water at 30 ng/L. In the present study, cyclic ion mobility–tandem mass spectrometry (cIMS-MS2) was used to identify 17 regulated and 52 unregulated PFAS in surface waters near a former firefighting training facility in Atlantic Canada, including 6 new PFAS that have not been previously reported in environmental waters: hydrido-ketone-5:2-fluorotelomer sulfonate (FTS), ketone-8:2-FTS, unsaturated 8:2-FTS, N-methyl-perfluorohexane sulfonamido sulfinate, N-methyl-perfluorooctane sulfonamido sulfinate, and perfluorohexane sulfonamido propionate. Semi-quantitation of unregulated PFAS was enabled by a machine-learning model validated using a set of 21 targeted PFAS (R2 > 0.95). The total concentration of PFAS declined from 2500 ng/L to 364 ng/L as the surface water entered the North Atlantic approximately 5 km away from the hotspot. Seven of forty-two drinking water wells located along a 5 km transect from the source were characterized by exceedances between 30 and 191 ng/L. Twenty-seven PFAS were identified in the wells, including 13 that are unregulated and 5 that result from (bio)transformation of AFFF. While the fraction of unregulated PFAS was low (<18%), these transformation products may inform forensic studies aimed at establishing links between the source of pollution and its receptors.

articles.title:
Anticipating the
Environmental Impact of AI-Enhanced
Robotics and Automation

Correction to “A
Review: Mechanisms, Processes
and Design Principles of Recycling Spent Lithium-Ion Battery and Biomass”

Divergent Catalytic
Strategies of Group-6 Propane
Monooxygenases in Propane-Stimulated 1,4-Dioxane Biodegradation
articles.abstract: Abstract Group-6 propane monooxygenases (PRMs) catalyze the initial oxidation of 1,4-dioxane (dioxane), a widespread contaminant of emerging concern. Because their expression can be induced by propane, an inexpensive and readily deliverable substrate, PRM-containing microorganisms offer a distinct advantage for propane-based biostimulation strategies targeting dioxane removal. However, functional differences among PRMs from the three major phylogenetic clusters remain poorly understood. Here, three PRMs from Mycobacterium dioxanotrophicus PH-06, Mycobacterium marinum E11, and Mycobacterium sp. ENV421, representing phylogenetic clusters, PRM-I, PRM-II, and PRM-III, respectively, were heterologously expressed in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc2155. ENV421 PRM-III exhibited low substrate affinity but high catalytic capacity toward both dioxane and propane, and moderate resistance to chlorinated solvent inhibition. In contrast, E11 PRM-II displayed high affinity but lower capacity and greater inhibitor sensitivity. PH-06 PRM-I showed comparatively stronger activity toward dioxane than propane relative to the other PRMs. Protein structure analysis suggested that variation in substrate affinity and catalytic turnover is consistent with differences in active-site pocket hydrophobicity, rigidity, and catalytic geometry. Phylogenetic and compositional analyses further suggested horizontal transfer in Clusters I and III. Together, these results highlight substantial functional diversity among group-6 PRMs and offer mechanistic insights for optimizing microbial populations for effective propane-stimulated bioremediation of dioxane.

articles.title:
Reducing PFAS Mobility
and Plant Uptake in Agricultural
Soils via Biochar Amendment
articles.abstract: Abstract Biochar amendment represents a promising in situ strategy for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) mitigation, yet its performance under realistic field conditions remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated PFAS fate in soil–plant–leachate systems under irrigation-water- and biosolids-derived contamination settings. Pinewood biochar (PBC) significantly (P = 0.05) reduced PFAS leaching and plant uptake more so than biosolids-derived biochar (BBC), driven by its higher point of zero charge (PZC), C/H and C/O ratios, and specific surface area, with the strongest mitigation observed for PFHxS and PFOA. Air oxidation and iron oxide modification of PBC further suppressed short-chain PFAS accumulation in plants. Among the tested materials, air-oxidized PBC exhibited the highest mitigation efficiency (ME), reducing leaf bioconcentration factors (BCFs) of PFHxS and PFOA by 1328.5-fold and 285.3-fold, respectively, and suppressing perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) accumulation by 150.8-fold, attributable to enhanced surface area, electrostatic attraction, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. Dissolved organic matter (DOM) released from biosolids increased the mobility of PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, and PFHxS while reducing the bioavailability and translocation of PFNA and PFOS. Collectively, this work demonstrates that PFAS mitigation by biochar is governed by molecular structures, input pathways, and DOM interactions, providing mechanistic insight for targeted biochar deployment in PFAS-impacted agroecosystems.

articles.title:
Toward
Recreating the Breath of Cities in the Atmospheric
Simulation Chamber SAPHIR
articles.abstract: Abstract Atmospheric simulation chambers are essential for studying oxidation processes, yet many experiments rely on single-precursor systems at concentrations that limit their representativeness for the chemical complexity of urban air. Here, we present a framework linking emission inventories, chamber experiments, and field observations by constructing emission fingerprints of major urban sources, including vegetation, volatile chemical products, cooking emissions, and gasoline and diesel exhaust. Applied during the CHANEL campaign in the SAPHIR outdoor chamber, these fingerprints advanced toward reproducing gas-phase mixtures representative of Los Angeles (gasoline-dominated traffic), a diesel-dominated city, and a future low-vehicle-emission scenario. The resulting mixtures generated peroxy-to-hydroperoxy radical ratios (RO2/HO2) close to unity, bimolecular RO2 lifetimes comparable with urban atmospheric observations, although lower NO levels favored RO2 + HO2 over RO2 + NO reactions. Comparison with aircraft measurements over Los Angeles using ammonium (NH4+) chemical ionization mass spectrometry showed reasonable agreement, with 465 organic product ions detected in both data sets, representing 78% of the product ions observed in the ambient air. Furthermore, 87% of common product ions agreed within a factor of 3 of the linear correlation, demonstrating that chamber experiments can capture key aspects of both atmospherically relevant radical chemistry and the oxidation product diversity of urban air.

articles.title:
Elevated Outdoor
O3 Can Sustain New Particle
Formation and Growth Indoors
articles.abstract: Abstract Ultrafine particles and submicron aerosol mass negatively impact human health; while indoor primary sources are known, secondary aerosol formation from oxidation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) is an important, but less understood, exposure source. Previous studies have suggested that indoor new particle formation (NPF) and growth are ozone-limited. However, we find that in an authentic aged unoccupied office in a region with high outdoor O3 concentrations, sufficient O3 is transported indoors that NPF and growth are instead limited by the availability of VOCs. Mechanical ventilation continuously supplies O3 in the summertime and sustains the subsequent growth so that particle growth rates upon the addition of limonene range from 20 to 100 nm h–1─rates 1–2 orders of magnitude greater than those observed outdoors. Additionally, we observe meaningful mass contributions from the growth of newly formed particles. Household use of limonene-containing products in rooms with elevated ozone─either from ozone-producing remediation and germicidal UV technologies, or during outdoor ozone exceedance events─will produce ultrafine particles and increase particle mass. The effect of ventilated O3 from outdoors on particle formation and growth highlights the value of continued efforts to reduce outdoor O3 pollution for moderating both indoor and outdoor sources of secondary pollutants.

articles.title:
Selective Destabilization
of Mineral-Protected Organic
Carbon Accompanies Iron Reduction across a Coastal Wetland Salinity
Gradient
articles.abstract: Abstract Climate-driven seawater intrusion is intensifying salinization in coastal wetlands, but its consequences for the stability of sediment organic carbon (OC) remain poorly constrained. Here, we combined field observations along a natural salinity gradient with spectroscopic and mineralogical analyses, mineral sorption–desorption experiments, and manipulative incubations to examine the stability of mineral-protected OC. Salt-marsh sediments contained 9.23% less OC than freshwater sediments, with a disproportionate difference in reactive iron-bound OC (FeR-OC). Across the 36 independent field plots, FeR-OC represented 9.80–22.95% of total OC, while the FW–SM FeR-OC difference was numerically equivalent to 64.28% of the corresponding bulk-OC difference. This disproportionate response was associated with a shift from reactive Fe(III)-bearing phases toward Fe(II)-rich products, as well as a weakening of mineral protection, supported by spectroscopic, mineralogical, and geochemical evidence. In salt-marsh incubations, molybdate addition decreased FeR-OC mobilization by 39.51%, identifying a molybdate-sensitive contribution consistent with the sulfate-reduction branch. Together, these results support an iron-unlocking pathway in sulfate-rich coastal wetlands, in which Fe reduction weakens mineral protection and mobilizes previously stabilized OC. This mechanism identifies iron-mediated mineral protection as an important geochemical vulnerability of blue carbon under increasing seawater influence, while the subsequent mineralization, export, or recapture of mobilized OC remains unresolved.

articles.title:
Catalyst
or Bystander? Disentangling True Catalytic
Effects from Confounding Phenomena in Ozone-Based Wastewater Treatment
articles.abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous catalytic ozonation has generated thousands of publications over two decades, with these publications articulating a consistent narrative: catalysts enhance ozone decomposition, generate hydroxyl radicals (or other reactive species), and improve contaminant removal beyond that achievable by use of ozone alone. Despite this narrative, performance gains demonstrated at laboratory scale are routinely inconsistent and poorly reproduced at pilot and industrial scale. This perspective argues that the field suffers from a systematic attribution problem with observed enhancements frequently misattributed to catalytic activity when, instead, they arise from gas–liquid mass transfer modification, pH effects, and/or metal leaching driving homogeneous reactions. Using quantitative modeling, we further demonstrate that faster catalyst-mediated reaction kinetics alone may not translate into meaningful process-level benefits, particularly in full-scale reactors where relatively long hydraulic retention times and constraints on O3 gas–liquid mass transfer can diminish the advantage of kinetic acceleration. A sustained catalytic advantage at scale, therefore, requires not only kinetic acceleration but also more efficient utilization of ozone, an important distinction that has received limited attention in the HCO literature. Based on these findings, we propose a framework that will assist in distinguishing true catalytic pathways from various confounders and will help establish process-relevant benefit of HCO at scale. Overall, this perspective establishes a more rigorous evidentiary basis for translating catalytic activity into reliable wastewater treatment performance.
